content_text: Couldn’t agree more. It strikes me that most AI adoption in finance has focused on automating or accelerating existing workflows, rather than questioning whether those workflows are optimal in the first place. As an analyst, I understand the appeal of getting to an answer faster. But surely the more interesting question is whether AI can help us arrive at fundamentally better answers? I’ve always been fascinated by the idea of an interconnected investment brain. Something akin to Obsidian, but purpose-built for investing, where companies, industries, themes, mental models, investment hypotheses and evidence exist within a continuously evolving knowledge graph. I’ve actually started experimenting with a prototype of this concept, which I’m calling Labyrinth. Imagine discovering something material about one business and being able to trace its implications across an entire network of companies, assumptions and investment theses. Rather than research existing in isolated notes, PDFs and spreadsheets, knowledge becomes interconnected, cumulative and increasingly useful. Now combine that with probabilistic modelling. Instead of a financial model producing a single target price based on point estimates, imagine one that represents a distribution of possible outcomes, understands the dependencies between assumptions and updates those probabilities as new evidence emerges. The analyst’s role shifts from manually maintaining models and processing information towards challenging assumptions, evaluating evidence and exercising judgement. I suspect Excel will eventually become less central to the investment process, replaced by something more dynamic, interconnected and probabilistic. Perhaps the biggest opportunity for AI in investing isn’t helping us do the same work faster. It’s fundamentally changing how we think, connect information and make decisions under uncertainty.
